identity.title: ALMA Thermal Observations of a Proposed Plume Source Region on Europa

paper_type_evidence.quote: We present a daytime thermal image of Europa taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array.

evidence.loc: Fits to ALMA and Galileo PPR Observations
evidence.quote: centered on 276$\degree$ W and 16.8$\degree$ S, which is coincident with the Galileo thermal anomaly in the potential plume source region

question.value: Is the Galileo PPR nighttime thermal excess near Pwyll Crater caused by excess endogenic heat flow (plume source) or by a local thermal inertia variation?

evidence.quote: evaluate whether the anomaly is best explained by variation in the thermal inertia or whether it is truly indicative of an endogenic hot spot.
ADS/JAO.ALMA#2015.1.01302.S
The observation described in this paper was taken in Band 6, near 230 GHz, in the “continuum” (or “TDM”) mode, with the standard frequency tuning.

frequencies_and_spectral_setup.value: four SPWs: 224–226, 226–228, 240–242, 242–244 GHz; effective frequency 233 GHz

evidence.quote: The observations described herein were undertaken with the 12-m array

configurations.value: C36-7, 50 antennas, max useable spacing ~5 km

evidence.quote: ALMA had 50 available antennas in its C36-7 configuration, with a maximum useable antenna spacing of $\sim$ 5 km.
deconvolved Europa image with the 0.05" effective resolution of the interferometer
We observed Europa with ALMA on November 27 of 2015 from 10:00 to 10:40 UTC.

method.value: Linear correlation between USGS basemap greyscale and Voyager normal albedos

evidence.quote: The greyscale values and approximate normal albedos correlate linearly with an $R^2$ of .92 and a standard deviation of .03

assumptions.value: Normal albedos taken as hemispherical (phase integral 1.01)

evidence.quote: we take these normal albedos as approximate hemispherical albedos

We then find the greyscale value of each corresponding point in the USGS basemap and use the resulting linear correlation to get an approximate wavelength-integrated normal albedo for each point in the USGS map.

method.value: 1D heat diffusion, grid over thermal inertia and emissivity, minimizing sum of squared residuals over region covered by both ALMA and PPR; model smoothed to beam / 140 km

evidence.quote: We define the thickness of the top layer to be $d/30$, with the thickness of each subsequent layer increasing by a factor of 1.2.

findings_qualitative.value: Pwyll region is warm at night and cold by day relative to model, indicating thermal inertia variation

evidence.loc: 4 Fits to ALMA and Galileo PPR Observations
evidence.quote: shows up as anomalously hot at night and cold during the day. This pattern is suggestive of a variation in the local thermal inertia.

claims.hypothesis: The nighttime thermal anomaly is due to endogenic heat flow
claims.experiment: Fit ALMA day and PPR night brightness temperatures with a heat-flux increase
claims.result: Matching night gives daytime temperature far too high; only works with 23% albedo increase (4 sigma)
claims.finding: Endogenic heating alone cannot explain the anomaly

evidence.loc: 4 Fits to ALMA and Galileo PPR Observations
evidence.quote: we are unable to successfully fit both brightness temperatures with a subsurface hot spot.

claims.hypothesis: A local thermal inertia increase explains the anomaly
claims.experiment: Fit both data points raising thermal inertia and albedo
claims.result: Inertia 95 to 140 with albedo 0.56 to 0.59 matches both
claims.finding: Anomaly most likely a thermal inertia variation, perhaps from Pwyll ejecta

evidence.quote: We therefore conclude that the nighttime Galileo thermal anomaly is most likely explained by a variation in the local surface thermal inertia

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Anomaly was endogenic at Galileo time (1998) but cooled by 2015; cannot be ruled out

evidence.loc: 4 Fits to ALMA and Galileo PPR Observations
evidence.quote: We cannot rule out the possibility that the region associated with the thermal anomaly was anomalously warm due to endogenic heat at the time of the Galileo observation in 1998, but has since cooled.

limitations_admitted.value: Simple homogeneous model; emissivities at ALMA and PPR wavelengths unknown

evidence.quote: However, the relevant emissivities for Europa-like conditions and compositions are not known.

referee_caveats_inferred: Only two data points constrain the local fit, with no stated uncertainties
Equal emissivity at 1.3 mm and 27.5 micron is assumed and strongly affects brightness temperatures
Absolute ALMA flux calibration for a resolved moving target not discussed
